# Community Management vs Social Media Management

Source: https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-social-media-management/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-18 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: Social media management is editorial work: the company's voice on its own accounts, measured by reach, response and traffic. Community management is hosting work: members' voices in spaces the company runs, measured by returning members and how much they help each other. Job descriptions routinely merge the two, and the evidence suggests the merged role is already stretched: CMX's 2025 survey found around 30% of community teams are one person. When one person holds both, the job that gets done depends on their temperament, not the company's needs.

## Key points

- Social media management publishes the company's voice; community management hosts other people's voices.
- The measures differ: reach, engagement and response time for social; returning members and member-to-member help for community.
- About three-quarters of consumers expect a brand to reply on social within 24 hours, which pulls a combined role towards the public feed.
- Only 24% of community professionals in CMX's 2025 survey could confidently quantify their community's value, so the community half is the easier one to neglect.
- Decide which job is primary before writing the job description, and say what will be secondary.

Job descriptions routinely ask for a "community and social media manager", as though the two were one skill with two channels. They are different jobs, with different daily work, different measures and different temperaments. A person good at one is frequently poor at the other. This guide sits alongside our hub on [building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/), which covers what a community needs once you have decided to run one.

## Social media management: a publication

The job is to represent the company on its own social accounts. Plan and publish content, adapt the company's messages to each platform's format, respond to public comments and mentions, monitor conversation about the brand, coordinate with founders and executives on their accounts, and report on reach and engagement.

The response part of the job is now an expectation with a clock on it. Sprout Social's 2025 Index found about three-quarters of consumers expect a brand to respond within 24 hours or sooner, and its Q4 2025 Pulse survey found 51% of people who reach out publicly expect a public acknowledgement before being moved to a private message. Those are vendor surveys, but the direction is clear: the public feed generates a queue, and the queue has a deadline.

The temperament is editorial. Good social managers are writers and editors who understand format, timing and platform behaviour. They are producing a publication. Our playbook on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) applies to their output: every post should have a reader, a purpose and a next action.

## Community management: an institution

The job is to build and maintain a group of people who participate with one another, in spaces the company hosts or convenes: a Discord, a forum, a customer group, an ambassador programme, working sessions, events. Welcome new members, design the ways people can contribute, moderate, resolve conflicts, surface what members are saying to the company and recognise contribution.

The measures are about members, not the company: returning active members, member-to-member interaction against staff-to-member, unique contributors, time to first useful response, movement up the participation ladder, and knowledge or value created by members.

These measures are harder to tie to money, and the profession knows it. CMX's 2025 Community Industry Report, a survey of 589 community professionals, found only 24% could confidently quantify the value of their community, and "difficulty proving ROI to justify budget" was the top budget challenge at 37%. Where community and customer data were connected in the CRM, teams were twice as likely to rate their impact extremely successful (24% against 11.5%).

The temperament is hosting. Good community managers are facilitators who are comfortable letting others speak, who notice individuals and who can hold a room. They are running an institution, not a publication.

|  | Social media management | Community management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Whose voice | The company's | The members' |
| Where | The company's own accounts on public platforms | Spaces the company hosts or convenes |
| Daily work | Plan, write, publish, reply, monitor | Welcome, moderate, connect, recognise, escalate |
| Core measures | Reach, engagement, relevant follower growth, traffic, response time | Returning members, member-to-member help, contributors, time to first useful response |
| Time horizon | Days and weeks | Quarters |
| Temperament | Editor | Host |
| Typical failure | Generic content on every platform | An announcement channel with a member count |

## Why combining them fails

The daily work competes. A publishing schedule and community presence both demand attention at the same hours, and the public queue is louder. When a mention needs a reply within the day and a quiet member's first question can wait, the quiet member waits.

The measures pull in different directions. A social manager is rewarded for the company's voice being heard. A community manager is rewarded for members' voices being heard, including when the company is not in the conversation at all. One report cannot serve both without one half becoming a footnote.

The skills rarely coincide. The editor who writes a sharp thread is not automatically the host who makes a quiet member feel welcome, and the host who can calm an argument is not automatically the writer who can make a product launch land on five platforms.

The staffing data makes the risk concrete. CMX found around 30% of community teams are a single person, and 17% of respondents said no one in their organisation works full time on community, the highest share the survey has recorded. Marketing was the most common reporting line at 31%, ahead of customer success and support at 19%. A one-person community function reporting into marketing is the role most likely to be asked to "also run social", and the least able to absorb it.

> When one person holds both jobs, which one gets done depends on their temperament, not on what the company needs.

## What each requires from the company

Social media management requires a point of view, a voice guide, access to the people whose thinking the content represents, and a decision about which platforms matter. Without those, the manager produces generic content on every platform. Our piece on [founder, brand and community accounts](https://lowob.com/research/founder-brand-community-social-strategy/) covers how to divide the voice between people and the company.

Community management requires a reason for people to participate with one another, a decision about what the community is for, consequential roles for members and patience measured in quarters. It also requires operating support the company often forgets. Discord's own moderation guidance recommends letting automation handle routine issues around the clock while keeping judgment calls with people, turning recurring questions into a read-only FAQ channel, and keeping enforcement "as fair and consistent as possible". That is a process, not a posting rota. Without it, the manager runs an announcement channel with a member count, the failure our piece on [community as a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) describes.

## How to staff by company type

For most small companies: one editorial person for social, part-time or shared with content, and a decision about whether a community is warranted at all. Many companies need excellent social presence and customer support and do not need a member-led community, and forcing one wastes a hire.

Where a community is warranted, hire for hosting, not for writing, and give the role a measurable purpose. CMX's data on objectives is a useful starting list: teams focused on support most often measured active users (41%) and case deflection (38%), teams focused on retention measured customer retention (72%), and teams focused on product feedback measured product ideas (71%). Pick one objective and its measure before the hire starts.

| Company situation | Usually primary | Usually secondary | Staffing pattern |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Founder with a following | Social, partly the founder's own | Community | Editorial support for the founder; community only if members ask for it |
| Web3 project | Community | Social | A host first, with social shared with content or the founder |
| Enterprise fintech | Social and executive presence | Community, often customer advisory groups | An editor first; a small customer group run by customer success |
| B2B SaaS with an active user base | Depends on the support model | The other | Two roles once both have a measurable purpose |

Where both are needed, they are two roles, or one role with a clear primary and an honest acknowledgment of what will be secondary. The [shift from founder-led to team-led marketing](https://lowob.com/research/from-founder-led-to-team-led-marketing/) is often the moment this decision has to be made explicitly, because the founder stops covering one of the jobs by default.

## lowob takeaways

- **Different jobs.** Social is editorial and publishes the company's voice; community is hosting and builds members' voices.
- **Different clocks.** Social replies are expected within a day; community value shows up over quarters, so the community half is neglected first.
- **Different measures.** Report reach and response time for social, and returning members and member-to-member help for community.
- **Decide the primary.** For a Web3 project community is usually primary; for an enterprise fintech, social usually is.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between a community manager and a social media manager?

A social media manager represents the company on its own accounts and is measured by reach, engagement and response time. A community manager builds a group whose members participate with one another in company-hosted spaces and is measured by returning members and member-to-member help.

### Should one person handle both community and social media?

Usually not. The work competes for the same hours, the public feed carries a same-day response expectation, and the skills rarely coincide, so one job tends to be neglected. If one person must do both, name the primary job in writing.

### Does every startup need a community manager?

No. Many companies need excellent social presence and customer support and do not need a member-led community. Hire a community manager only when there is a reason for members to help each other and a measure for whether they do.

### How do you measure a community manager's performance?

Against one stated objective: active users and case deflection for a support community, retention for a customer community, product ideas for a feedback community. Add returning members and time to first useful response as health measures.

## Next Move

Before you post the next "community and social" job description, write one sentence naming which job is primary and the single measure it will be judged on. If you cannot name a community measure, hire for social and leave community for later.
